title: Validation and Overfitting
tagline: Rolling and expanding walk-forward, purging, embargoes, grid search, sequential search and the deflated Sharpe ratio
summary: A parameter chosen on the same sample that is then quoted as evidence has not been tested. This course builds walk-forward protocols — rolling, expanding and anchored — inserts a purge and an embargo where labels overlap, and treats grid search and a sequential model-based search as part of the experiment. The deflated Sharpe ratio is derived as a correction for selection, and the last chapter says what a stack of folds still does not prove.
overview: The open library’s walk-forward examples are unusually honest about their own status. The pages describe rolling, expanding and anchored splits, with a purge before the test window, and they label the output as slice diagnostics rather than as independent out-of-sample evidence. This course teaches the machinery those pages are using, and it teaches the caveat in the same chapter as the machinery.

A walk-forward split is a sequence of training windows and later test windows. Rolling windows keep a fixed training length. Expanding windows use all history up to the split. An anchored design adds an explicit exclusion, fixed or proportional, so that a label which looks past the split does not train on data that overlap the test. That exclusion is the purge. An embargo adds a further gap when serial dependence would leak information across the boundary. López de Prado’s account is the one followed here.

Search is not validation. A 3 by 3 grid of moving-average windows, scored by the in-sample Sharpe ratio, is nine experiments. A sequential search such as the TPE sampler used by Optuna spends a budget of trials on the same history. The trial that wins is the most selected, not the most confirmed. Confirmation is a later walk-forward of the frozen choice, and even that confirmation is one path through one asset class.

The deflated Sharpe ratio, following Bailey and López de Prado, adjusts a reported Sharpe for the number of trials, the length of the sample and non-normality. The course works the formula on small numbers. It does not produce a threshold above which a rule should be traded.
outcomes: Construct a rolling and an expanding walk-forward split and state what is known at each training date.
Place a purge and an embargo between train and test when labels or dependence overlap the boundary.
Count the number of trials in a grid and explain why the best in-sample cell is a selected statistic.
Describe a sequential model-based search at the level of its objective and its trial budget, and separate the search from a later test of the winner.
Compute a deflated Sharpe ratio from a reported Sharpe, a trial count and a sample length under the stated assumptions.
Explain why dozens of folds on one history are not dozens of independent replications.

history.title: A reality check that includes the search
history.detail: White’s bootstrap reality check tests the best rule found by snooping against the null that none of the tried rules has value. It is the predecessor of later deflators.

history.title: Random search as a baseline
history.detail: Bergstra and Bengio showed that random search is a strong and simple baseline for hyperparameter optimisation. A grid is not the only search, and it is not free of multiplicity.

history.title: The deflated Sharpe ratio
history.detail: Bailey and López de Prado corrected a Sharpe ratio for selection bias, the number of trials and non-normal returns.

history.title: Purged cross-validation
history.detail: López de Prado’s book set out purged and embargoed cross-validation for financial labels that overlap in time. The walk-forward examples in the open library are a practical cousin of that design.

history.title: Optuna and the TPE sampler
history.detail: Akiba, Sano, Yanase, Ohta and Koyama released Optuna, whose Tree-structured Parzen Estimator is the sequential sampler the library’s fifth walk-forward example uses. The paper is about the optimiser, not about trading.
